articles.title: Science news in review: Oct. 5
articles.description: Here's this week's science news in review: Fungicidal activity and common skin infections In a study published in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology, researchers found that an extract from Cistus salviifolius, a Mediterranean rockrose used traditionally for skin conditions, can kill several types of dermatophytes (the fungi responsible for ringworm and other skin, hair and nail infections). The extract was particularly effective against Trichophyton rubrum, one of the most common causes of fungal skin infections, and Microsporum canis, which spreads from animals to humans. Chemical analysis showed that the extract contains large amounts of polyphenols, including tannins and flavonoids. Interestingly, the effect was not universal: the extract did not show significant activity against the yeast Candida albicans at the concentrations tested, suggesting that its antifungal action may only be effective against certain groups of fungi. The researchers also examined how the extract damages fungal cells . Electron microscopy showed major structural changes, including disruption of cellular organization, membrane separation and formation of large vacuoles. Even more promising, the extract was tested in a laboratory-grown model of human epidermis. Treatment reduced the amount of fungus invading the tissue, helped preserve the skin barrier and lowered the inflammatory response without significantly harming the skin cells themselves. These findings provide a foundation for developing standardized creams or gels and eventually testing their efficacy in clinical trials. Cosmic flashes and dead stars In a recent study , astronomers may have identified a new way to recognize collisions between neutron stars . Traditionally, neutron star mergers are associated with extremely short bursts of gamma rays , often lasting less than two seconds. However, researchers investigated an unusual event called EP250704a/GRB 250704B , detected in July 2025, that produced a roughly half-second gamma-ray burst but continued emitting bright X-rays for almost 10 minutes. This was the longest lasting prompt X-ray emission yet observed from a suspected neutron-star merger. The researchers believe the collision may have produced a magentar , a rapidly spinning neutron star with an extraordinarily strong magnetic field. A magnetar could continue releasing huge amounts of energy after the original collision, explaining why the X-ray signal lasted much longer than a normal short gamma-ray burst. Importantly, astronomers found no evidence of the bright supernova that would usually accompany the collapse of a massive star, strengthening the argument that two neutron stars merged instead. The discovery suggests that some mysterious, fast X-ray transients previously detected throughout the universe could actually be hidden neutron-star mergers. Tsunami warnings and Pacific ringing Researchers studying the magnitude 8.8 Kamchatka earthquake of July 29, 2025 found that the resulting tsunami continued producing measurable oscillations throughout the Pacific Ocean for more than 10 hours. To study the event, scientists compared a computer simulation based only on the earthquake's rupture with measurements from six deep-ocean DART tsunami-monitoring stations. Their model performed remarkably well: predicted arrival times were within about a minute of the actual measurements, while maximum wave heights differed by only about 6 centimeters on average. The results indicate that the earthquake itself was sufficient to explain the observed tsunami without needing to invoke another fault rupture or an underwater landslide. Near the source, the event was still extremely powerful, with water reaching approximately 19 meters above sea level on parts of the Kuril Islands . The key discovery came after the initial waves passed. The researchers found that tsunami energy remained concentrated in waves with periods of roughly 30-80 minutes for more than 10 hours, meaning the Pacific behaved somewhat like a giant bell that continued vibrating long after being struck. This rhythm could be important for improving tsunami warnings because bays and harbors also have their own natural oscillation periods. If the period of an incoming tsunami matches a harbor's natural period, resonance can cause water levels inside that harbor to become much larger than the waves in the open ocean. Researchers suggest that future warnings could consider not only how high a tsunami is and when it will arrive but also its dominant wave periods to better predict which coastlines and harbors are most vulnerable to dangerous amplification.

articles.title: To watch and watch for: Week of Oct. 4
articles.description: The first week of October has a lot to offer in terms of change: some colder temperatures, a bit of windier weather and a truer sense of fall truly setting in. As fall begins, you may be looking for new or exciting experiences with the changing seasons. Whether you're looking for a new film or novel, we've got you covered with suggestions for you. Before the spooky season officially kicks off, enjoy the start of this month with these recommendations for what to fill your time with! Who needs a remake of Blade ridden with production issues when Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother exists instead? Thanks to the ashes of the scrapped Marvel production , Academy Award winner Mahershala Ali returns to the big screen in this new action thriller, already professionally trained and toned for the lead role. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother follows a devoutly religious hitman who must contend with his faith, work and fatherhood as he makes a perilous adventure through Houston for the sake of his children. The film seems to be a novel action picture concerned with deeper questions about motivation and duty. In How to Look Away: On American Cruelty and the Refusal to Disappear , award-winning contributor to The Guardian and The New York Times Daniel Peña combines memoir with journalism and cultural criticism to convey an intriguing account of the American identity. From examining conspiracy theories to Cold War paranoia to writing about his experiences in Mexico and the United States, Pẽna examines what it takes to disappear in the American project and offers a clarifying look into the strained politics of America. Troye Sivan's fourth studio album, She's the Best , is a love letter to the women in the pop artist's life. The lead single of the album shares the same name, and it's a portrait of an unnamed woman who Sivan adores. The single "She's the Best" features a more alternative sound with distortive guitars than the usual dance-pop his songs have. However, She's the Best will certainly be as dance-worthy as the rest of his discography and worth a listen. At Baltimore's Black Arts and Public Humanities with Mary Rizzo and Rejjia Camphor , Associate Professor Mary Rizzo from the History Department at Rutgers University will be in conversation with Baltimore artist, activist and organizer Rejjia Camphor about Black arts and public history in Baltimore. Specifically, this event will talk about vernacular poetry and the revitalization of a Black grassroots poetry magazine published in Baltimore through a project called the Chicory Revitalization Project. Camphor's new co-authored book studying this project will also be discussed. Don't miss this conversation detailing the history of an undiscussed part of Baltimore's art scene! If nothing above seemed quite compelling, we have a full list of other options to browse through: To watch... articles.title: Nobel Statistics: A look at the relationship between Hopkins and the Prize
articles.description: As the world turns its ears toward Stockholm for this year's Nobel Prize announcements, we have a chance to reflect upon and analyze the intertwined history of the esteemed prize-giving body with our university. Though the exact criteria through which certain victors can be "claimed" may vary, Hopkins itself officially lists 29 affiliated winners as of September 2026. These winners span each category awarded, except for the prize in Literature , which has thus far eluded our community. These include - in decreasing order of the number of prizes linked to Hopkins - Physiology or Medicine , Physics , Chemistry , Economics and Peace . Of the three prizes for scientific fields, which will be the focus of this article, Hopkins claims connection to 24 winners. Notably, all Nobel laureates currently serving as members of the faculty - Peter Agre , Gregg Semenza and Adam Riess - fall under this number. To sketch a timeline, the Nobel Prize was first awarded in 1901 , around 25 years after the University's founding , with the first Hopkins associate receiving the award in 1919 (specifically Woodrow Wilson , winning for peace). James Franck would win the honor in 1925 for his analysis of the electron, and he later became a professor of Physics at Hopkins from 1935-1938. That said, the earliest winner of a scientific honor to have received a degree from Hopkins was Thomas Hunt Morgan , who completed his doctorate in Zoology at the University in 1890 and was awarded in 1933 for his foundational work with chromosomes. Tallying the count, 11 alumni who completed a degree program at Hopkins have received the recognition for their achievements in science. Of these alumni, 10 received their Ph.D. or M.D. at Hopkins, while two - Francis Peyton Rous (who received both his B.A. and M.D. degrees from Hopkins) and Martin Rodbell - acquired their undergraduate degree at this institution. It is worth noting the University's status as the first research university in the United States, having offered undergraduate programs alongside graduate programs since 1876 despite its initial emphasis on the latter . At the time of his award in 1933, Morgan was affiliated with the California Institute of Technology . Following that line of thinking, if we were to trace the affiliations of awardees, Hamilton O. Smith and Daniel Nathans in 1978 mark the first winners to have received the award while affiliated with Hopkins at the time, winning in Medicine for the discovery of restriction enzymes and their applications. Of the 24 laureates in science, 8 have won while holding a faculty or adjunct position at Hopkins, with 6 of them being recognized in the 21st century. Perhaps of greater interest than the affiliation of awardees at the time is what prizes were awarded for scientific research conducted at Hopkins. While delineating the exact boundaries between contributions from specific institutions can be a difficult, if not downright impossible, task, several awards mark notable findings obtained at the University. These include research leading to the discovery of aquaporins and restriction enzymes , key work on cells adapting to oxygen availability and significant innovations in our understanding of the visual system . Previous Nobel laureates have praised Hopkins as an environment in which to conduct prize-winning research, with Semenza explaining in a Hub staff report, "That's why I've stayed here my whole career, because I think this is the greatest place to do research". These research opportunities have continually attracted talent, as seen with Shimon Sakaguchi , who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine last year and conducted postdoctoral studies at Hopkins - although he has not been officially listed as an affiliated awardee by the University. Contributions by Hopkins scientists that were not directly recognized by the Nobel committee, such as several experimental physicists who assisted in work on the Higgs boson , have also been identified. Similar, less evident connections meriting additional notice are seen with other figures such as Hopkins alumni James Muller and James Cobey , whose experiences and education as medical students at the University played a role in their establishments of Nobel Peace Prize- winning organizations . Regarding current affiliates of the University, several have achieved other awards that are often linked to future Nobel laureates. For example, many winners of the Wolf Prize - such as Solomon Snyder , who conducted extensive research at Hopkins - have gone on to win Nobel Prizes . Graduates and members of the faculty like Bert Vogelstein , a professor of oncology, have also won several awards of note such as the Lasker Award and the Breakthrough Prize . In extrapolating any further conclusions from the data discussed here, prospective analysts must be wary of certain considerations. The Nobel Prize is an awards system based on annual selection by committee , and it has been accused of carrying its own biases and blind spots as well as being subject to internal politics . Its criteria, including traditional limits on the number of awardees and a refusal to award posthumously, further constrain its scope. Furthermore, the recognition (or lack thereof) of winners as university affiliates can be contested in several cases, as with Sakaguchi. Interrogations of our history with the award offer specific findings which, when applied with care and judgement, may yield broader insights and raise important questions about the University's engagement with the vast tapestry of the scientific endeavor.
